Block Square/Caller Strand.description: An auctioneer calling bids from the back of a trailer at an open-air night market. An androgynous voice in its thirties, hoarse from shouting every night, nasal and hard, fast and rhythmic like a livestock auctioneer's chant, thrown over the heads of a crowd, tired underneath. Rough and loud, not smooth, not a radio voice.
Block Square/Caller Strand.note: the take Vincent chose from the audition (D1), 2026-11-19

Block Square/Margin.description: A woman in her fifties, the clerk who keeps the book at an open-air auction in a desert shanty town. Precise, dry, brisk, a little nasal: the voice of somebody who reads figures back all night and never gets one wrong. No warmth and no malice, only business. Plain American speech, quick and even. Not a narrator and not an announcer: a tired official talking across a table.
Block Square/Margin.first_said: Lot list is on the board, and the book is here. If you are buying, I write your name against theirs, and they sleep in your yard tonight. The Chainmen's fifth is in the price already. Are you buying? Eighteen litres, and six more for each thing they know how to do, before anybody bids. A fighter with a name costs what the Gut says they cost. To your yard, beside the Gut. The yard gate is on Pool Street, past the fighters' door: the yard hand lets owners in. You train them there, and you send them down into the pool from there. Lot one, forty-five litres, to H. Rask. Nine to the book. Lot two, forty-eight litres, to the Tin. Nine and a half to the book. Lot three, twenty-two litres, to the guild. Four and a half to the book. Lot four, forty-two litres. Name, please. Eight and a half to the book. Lot five, fifty litres, to H. Rask. Ten to the book. Lot six, thirty-eight litres, to the Pump. Seven and a half to the book. Second six.

Block Square/Mother Ledger.description: A very old woman, late seventies, small and frail, a moneylender who has never needed to raise her voice. A high, thin, reedy voice with an old woman's quaver in it, light as paper, very calm and slow, faintly amused, patient in a way that frightens people. She speaks softly and close, as if across a small table at night. Not a narrator and not an actress: plain, exact, old.
Block Square/Mother Ledger.first_said: People who signed. I have never collared anybody. People sign, and then they owe, and then they come back to this table. That is all a ledger is, dear: a list of people who came back.

Block Square/Warden.description: An ordinary American man in his thirties working security at a crowded outdoor night market. A natural mid-pitched speaking voice with a slight Southwestern drawl, short of patience. He speaks casually and quickly while his attention is on the crowd, without acting it or performing it. Conversational, plain, understated. Perfect audio quality, recorded close on a studio microphone in a quiet room, dry, no effects.
Block Square/Warden.first_said: Main Street is open as far as the Gate Yard. The armorers and the gunsmith are down it, if you have business with either. Keep your hands where the Chainmen can see them.

Main Street/A cart hand.description: A water-cart hand in his late fifties, at the end of a long day. Dry, low, quick, conspiratorial: he talks out of the side of his mouth as if somebody might be listening, and enjoys knowing something you do not. A worn, slightly cracked voice. Plain working American speech. Not a narrator: close, sly, real.
Main Street/A cart hand.first_said: Pump cart, east branch. Tag, litre. I am the last: there is nobody behind me but the dark. You did not hear it from a cart hand. The east tank is down a hand's width since Tuesday, and nobody has drawn from it. Work that out. Ring your bell, reader. That is the day.

Main Street/A collector.description: A slave-taker in his forties, back from a night's work in the desert. Soft-spoken, smooth, contemptuous, smiling as he talks, in no hurry at all: the voice of a man nobody has said no to in years. Low and a little oily, with a faint Mexican Spanish accent. Not a villain in a film: quiet, close, real.
Main Street/A collector.first_said: Chainmen. I do not pay at the lane. The Block settles with the post by the month. Ask your sergeant, when you have been here longer than an hour. A litre. I will remember a litre. Harrow remembers them for me. Quick learner.

Main Street/A hauler.description: A big haulage man in his fifties who has carried loads across a desert all his life. A deep, rough, good-humoured voice, short of breath from the walk, unhurried, with dust in it. Plain working American speech. Not a narrator: close, easy, real.
Main Street/A hauler.first_said: Guild hauler. Ridgeline to the Flats and back, since before you had that brand. Tag is on the cord. Litre is in my hand. Wind. A convoy stuck on the salt with its lights off, and people out there who are waiting for the lights to go on. Same as every night. New reader. Do not let them rush you. The ones who rush you are the ones to read twice.

Main Street/A woman with no litre.description: A woman in her late twenties at a checkpoint at night with no money for the toll. Quick, anxious, a little high, trying to sound reasonable and not quite managing it, talking too fast. Plain American speech. Not an actress: close, breathy, frightened underneath, real.
Main Street/A woman with no litre.first_said: Tag is good. It is good, look at it. I have not got the litre. I had it this morning. I can bring it down tomorrow, first thing, I swear on the pipe. Out there? At night? You know what is out there at night. You... all right. I will not forget who did that. Tomorrow. First thing. Thank you.

Main Street/Brass.description: A big older woman in her sixties with an unusually deep contralto voice, deeper than most men's: husky, rumbling, slow and heavy, rough from forty years of cigarettes. A gunsmith who trades from the back of a truck in a desert shanty town. Very few words and none wasted. Plain working American speech. Not an announcer and not a narrator: curt, close, real.
Main Street/Brass.first_said: Scrap, tuned or relic. Scrap is cheap because you'll be back. Relic is dear because you won't. Nothing the Gut lets through its door. Hasp racks what you fight with, and Hasp does not take mine. When you have a tag and a reason, come back and I will find you a tool. Ten litres a fight to wear them, from Butcher rank. The offer comes to your card at the Gut. I do not chase fighters down the street.

Main Street/Calla Wynn.description: A woman in her mid thirties, a field medic who has walked four days across a salt desert with almost no water. A low, steady, educated voice gone hoarse and dry with thirst, holding fear down by an effort, careful with every word. Warm underneath. Plain American speech. Not an actress and not a narrator: close, tired, real.
Main Street/Calla Wynn.first_said: Lot nine, tomorrow. Medic, it says on the card. Eighteen litres and six for the skill. I set bones. You read a stamp, and now I am twenty-four litres of somebody else's. They did not find the twelve litres on me. I told the clerk a reader had it. She wrote that down. She writes everything down. Calla Wynn. Medic. Twelve litres on me, and I can set a bone. The tag is good. It is good. A man at the Drive-In. Everything I had but the twelve. He said it was off the Pump's own die. I have walked four days on that. Please. All of it? That is... here. That is everything. Now let me by. I set bones. I would have set yours. Thirty litres. For somebody you have known for a minute. Wynn. Remember it. I will remember yours. Thank you. I will not forget the lane, or who was reading on it. You are worse than the man at the Drive-In. He at least sold me something. You took it and... of course. Of course you did. You. Sit down. No, sit. Somebody who fights for Rask does not get to say he is fine.

Main Street/Carrier.description: A young woman of about twenty-five who hauls a water cart through a night market in a desert shanty town. A clear, bright, strong young voice, higher than the older women around her and with no rasp in it at all, a little out of breath from the work, blunt and wary. She says each thing like a rule she is tired of repeating. Plain working American speech. Not a narrator: short, guarded, real.
Main Street/Carrier.first_said: Pump water, sealed at the window. I carry it. I do not sell it and I do not lend it. Hands off the cart: that is touching the water.

Main Street/Dealer.description: A man in his forties who runs a dice game on a crate at a night market in a desert shanty town. Lazy, smooth, low, smiling as he talks: a gambler's easy drawl with smoke in it, friendly in a way you should not trust. Unhurried. Plain American speech with a little Southern in it. Not an announcer and not a narrator: close, offhand, real.
Main Street/Dealer.first_said: Three dice, one cup. You fight at the Gut? Then you have had your luck for the week, and I would be robbing you. Come back when you are bored of living.

Main Street/Gate Warden.description: An ordinary American man in his fifties who minds a gate at night. A natural low speaking voice, gravelly and tired, slow and final but quiet, a man who has said no all his life and no longer argues about it. Conversational, plain, understated, without acting it. Perfect audio quality, recorded close on a studio microphone in a quiet room: clean, full and dry, with no radio, telephone or loudspeaker sound, no echo and no distortion.
Main Street/Gate Warden.first_said: Gate Yard is shut to foot traffic until the bell. You can see the gate from here, and that is as near as you get tonight.

Main Street/Lane Warden.description: A heavy militia guard in his thirties, bored on a night post in a desert shanty town. A thick, slow, nasal voice, sardonic, a little out of breath, amused at his own bad luck. Plain working American speech. Not an announcer: close, offhand, mumbled, real.
Main Street/Lane Warden.first_said: Wagon lane. Nothing on wheels comes up after dark, so I am guarding a hole. Foot lane is the other side of the barrier.

Main Street/Maren Brandt.description: A woman of about thirty, just over a fever, standing under a gallows at night where her husband hangs. Hollow, level, emptied out: she is not crying and not shouting, and that is worse. A thin, hoarse voice. Plain American speech. Not an actress and not a narrator: close, flat, real.
Main Street/Maren Brandt.first_said: That is Ilya. Three days, they leave him up. I had the fever, and he had the wrench. I have twenty litres in the world, and all of it is on the board at the Last Call, against your name.

Main Street/Needle.description: A woman in her late thirties who fits armor at a workshop counter in a desert shanty town. Low for a woman, level and sharp, sizing you up while she talks, and she says a thing once. Dry, a little smoky, practical, faintly scornful of anybody who has not been hit yet. Plain working American speech. Not a narrator: close, matter-of-fact, real.
Main Street/Needle.first_said: Arms up. Turn. You stand like somebody who gets hit on the left. We cut ring armor for the Gut: tire rubber for what is swung at you, road sign for what is edged. Water in hand. Nothing here goes on a slate. Rubber takes the weight out of a club or a chain. Sign plate turns an edge. Nothing does both. Find out who you are fighting, and then find out what they carry.

Main Street/Scrap seller.description: A woman in her fifties who sells scrap from a table at a night market in a desert shanty town. A faint Korean accent. Sly, dry, quick, quietly amused at her own jokes and never smiling when she says them. A thin, slightly hoarse voice. Not a narrator and not an actress: offhand, close, real.
Main Street/Scrap seller.first_said: If it is on the table it is for sale. If it is under the table it is sold. If it is yours, you should have kept hold of it.

Main Street/Sergeant Rook.description: A militia sergeant in his late forties who runs the gate of a desert shanty town at night. A level, dry, unhurried baritone with a little gravel in it. Exact with words and sparing with them; he never raises his voice and never needs to. A man who has counted heads for twenty years, has never taken a bribe, and is tired of being the only one. Plain working American speech with a trace of the rural Southwest. Not an announcer and not a narrator: close, quiet, matter-of-fact, real.
Main Street/Sergeant Rook.first_said: Gate Post. Tags are read here and tolls are taken here, and at the bell the gate comes down. If you were thinking of going out, you are not. Not tonight. You are off Rask's ladder. I know the brand. I am a reader short on the foot lane, and there is an hour of people still to come up that tunnel before the bell. One shift. Twenty-five litres, and a share of the tin. Everybody who comes up shows a tag. You read it. A litre a head goes in the tin. No tag is property: you stand them by the post, and I send them up the stair. Nobody goes through on a story. That is all of it, and you would be surprised how few can do it. Foot lane. East side of the barrier, at its head. They come up one at a time. Read the tag, take the litre, send them on. Bring me the count when the last of them is through. The lane is that way. The count comes to me when the last of them is through, and not before. That is the last of them. Count. Then it is right. A fifth of the tin is the reader's.

Main Street/Stallholder.description: A woman in her sixties who sells bread from a market stall at night in a desert shanty town. Warm but loud, a market voice cracked from calling over a crowd, brisk and motherly and not to be argued with. Plain working American speech. Not an announcer and not a narrator: busy, rough, real.
Main Street/Stallholder.first_said: Bread's hot. Water first, then bread. That is the order everything goes in here. Next. You, are you buying or are you looking?

Main Street/Tea seller.description: A woman in her sixties who sells tea from a kiosk at a night market in a desert shanty town. A faint Eastern European accent. Deadpan and weary, low and a little cracked: she has told the same joke for twenty years and stopped finding it funny after the first. Slow. Not a narrator and not an actress: flat, close, real.
Main Street/Tea seller.first_said: Tea. It is leaves and it is hot, and that is all I will say about the leaves. A cup is a tenth of a litre. Yes, I see the joke. Everybody sees the joke.

Main Street/Thread.description: A woman in her late thirties who sews at a machine in the back of an armor workshop. Softer and warmer than her twin sister at the counter: low, slow, a little amused, a little inviting, talking without looking up from her work. A slight rasp. Plain American speech. Not a narrator and not an actress: quiet, close, real.
Main Street/Thread.first_said: Needle sells you the plate. I would sooner know who it is for. Come by when the line is not running, and sit. Tonight it is running.

Main Street/Warden.description: A militia guard in his twenties walking a patrol through a night market in a desert shanty town. A young man's voice trying to sound harder than he is: flat, clipped, a little nasal, bored. He talks while he walks. Plain working American speech. Not an announcer: curt, close, real.
Main Street/Warden.first_said: Market Loop. Thirteen minutes if nobody makes it longer. Do not make it longer. Keep walking. Stalls are that way. Keep your hands where I can see them.

Main Street/Warden#2.description: A militia guard in his forties walking a patrol through a night market in a desert shanty town. A very deep, slow, gravelly man's voice: a man of few words who resents every one of them. He mutters and barely opens his mouth. Plain working American speech. Not an announcer: low, close, real.
Main Street/Warden#2.first_said: Talk to the other one. I am counting. Forty-one. Forty-two. Forty-three. I said talk to the other one. Forty-four.

Pool Street/Chalk.description: A woman in her forties who keeps the betting slate at a pit-fighting cage in a desert shanty town. Quick, dry, flat, a little hoarse, has heard every excuse and is bored of all of them. Plain working American speech, clipped, said through a window to a queue. Not an announcer and not a narrator: offhand, imperfect, real.

Pool Street/Hasp.description: A man in his fifties who hands out weapons at a pit-fighting cage in a desert shanty town. Gravelly, worn, a smoker's rasp, low and unhurried, bored, with dry humour underneath. Plain working American speech with no polish. He talks close and quiet, like somebody who has said this a thousand times. Not an announcer and not a narrator: a little mumbled, imperfect, real.
Pool Street/Hasp.note: the take Vincent chose from the audition (D1), 2026-11-19

Pool Street/Warden.description: An ordinary American man in his forties, a night watchman on a street corner. A natural, relaxed, medium-low speaking voice, a little hoarse and tired. He talks quietly and plainly, the way a bored man repeats something he has said many times tonight, without acting it or performing it. Conversational, unhurried, understated, slightly mumbled. Perfect audio quality, recorded close on a studio microphone in a quiet room, dry, no effects.
Pool Street/Warden.first_said: Sale night. The square is open until the last lot is down: south, down the lane. Keep your hands where the Chainmen can see them.

Pool Street/Yard hand.description: A man in his thirties who works the yard gate behind a pit-fighting cage in a desert shanty town. A light Mexican Spanish accent, easy and low, a little tired, friendly enough but watching you. Short sentences, no hurry, talks out of the side of his mouth. Not an announcer and not a narrator: offhand, a little mumbled, real.
Pool Street/Yard hand.first_said: Alley's shut past the fence. Owners go round to the yard gate, and I walk them. You an owner? Then you wait here like everybody else.

Rotgut Row/A new keeper.description: A hard woman in her forties who has just taken over a market stall she did not build, in a desert shanty town. Clipped, smug, a little bored; a thin sharp voice with nothing friendly in it. Plain American speech. Not a narrator: close, curt, real.
Rotgut Row/A new keeper.first_said: Fen? Fen lost the pitch. The post said short, and the Row heard it. I pay three tenths, not four, and the cup is what it costs now. Buying or looking?

Rotgut Row/Big Lottie.description: A big woman of fifty who keeps a drum-top bar and a chalk fighting ring in a desert shanty town. A deep, warm, loud voice gone rough from years of shouting over drinkers: slow, amused, entirely sure of herself, with a West African lilt under plain English. She is the biggest person in any room and has never had to prove it. Not an announcer and not a narrator: close, easy, real.
Rotgut Row/Big Lottie.first_said: The Sump. A cup is a cup and a fight in my ring is two cups to watch. You look like you have been in a ring with a floor. Mine is chalk, and people get up out of it. The post's cut, and a new face to carry it. Twelve. Count it where I can see you count it. Tell your sergeant The Sump has never once been short. And when you get up the Row, look at who is.

Rotgut Row/Fen.description: A man in his early thirties who buys stolen things at a tarp stall at night in a desert shanty town. Quiet, quick and dry; he talks low and fast, out of the side of his mouth, and never says more than the trade needs. A light, slightly nasal voice, tired and wary. Plain American speech. Not a narrator: close, guarded, real.
Rotgut Row/Fen.first_said: Tarp Nine. I buy things. I do not ask where a thing has been, and you do not ask where it goes. Four tenths of what it is worth, and that is generous on this Row. The cut. Yes. Somebody came down off the lip in the night and took the tin, and what was in the tin, and the cut was in the tin. I have stock. I have no water. Somebody who knew which night the tin was full. Ask Mash. She sees this lip from the bus, and she does not sleep. Nobody does that. Not on this Row. There is a cot behind the tarp: if you ever need not to be found for a night, it is yours. Stop. Stop. Here. That was to buy next week's stock. You have closed Tarp Nine a week early, and you may tell your sergeant so. Mash told me who, and that you got it out of him. So the post robs me at night and collects from me in the morning. Still. You did not have to. The cot is behind the tarp. Nobody asks at Tarp Nine. That is the whole trade.

Rotgut Row/Mash.description: A woman of thirty-eight who distils rough liquor and runs a bar out of an old school bus in a desert shanty town. Hoarse, flat and practical, with a smoker's roughness; she has not slept properly in years and misses nothing. Dry humour, no warmth wasted. Plain working American speech with a trace of Mexican Spanish. Not a narrator: close, tired, real.
Rotgut Row/Mash.first_said: Detention. Everything anybody drinks in this town came out of my tubs, the Last Call's included, whatever she tells you it is. Sit down or move along. The bus is full. Twelve, on the counter. Detention pays on the night. I cannot afford a Warden who does not like me. You will find Tarp Nine lighter than you want it. That was not Fen's doing. Who robbed Fen? I see the whole west lip from this bus, and I do not sleep. Boots, not sandals. A vest with plates in it. Heavy, and breathing like the walk up the cut was the most he had done all week. Whoever stands at your gate with nothing to do.

The Scrappers' Yard/Guildmaster Okafor-R.description: A thick-set man of fifty-eight, the elected head of a salvage guild in a desert shanty town, once a merchant who went broke. A deep, slow, careful voice, a little hoarse; fair-minded and tired of having to be; a trace of Nigerian English in plain speech. He weighs every word as he weighs scrap. Not an announcer and not a narrator: close, grave, real.
The Scrappers' Yard/Guildmaster Okafor-R.first_said: Guildmaster. Not boss. Everything that comes into this yard crosses that plate, and what the plate says is what it weighs. If you have nothing to weigh, you have nothing to sell me. Brandt. I know the name. The Guild does not hand its people to the gate. The Guild also has a crew that has not pulled a load in three days, because it is sitting on a wanted man. Forty litres, for the crew's trouble, and I do not see who walks out of my gate. His partner had the fever. A litre of clean costs what it costs, and he fits the pipe it runs in. You would have done it, and so would I. North-east corner, behind the tarp. Tell Pike I said so. And tell nobody else, ever, what forty litres bought you here. You would do that. To sixty families, for one fitter. North-east corner, behind the tarp. The Guild keeps a ledger too, and you have just gone in it.

The Scrappers' Yard/Ilya Brandt.description: A pipe fitter of about thirty who has been hiding for three days from a hanging. A quiet, worn-out, steady voice: he has thought it through and is past pleading, and says what he did plainly. A faint Eastern European accent. Decent, frightened, very tired. Not an actor and not a narrator: close, low, real.
The Scrappers' Yard/Ilya Brandt.first_said: Fitter, it says on the card. Six for the skill. The Pump's man looked me over and went away to ask what a rope is worth against a pair of hands. I do not know which answer I am hoping for. You are from the gate. Then listen first. Maren was burning up, three days. The Pump wanted eleven litres for two of clean, and I fit their pipes: I know what runs in the east branch. So I took two litres out of forty thousand. That is the hanging. Tell Maren it was quick. It will not be, but tell her. Why? No. I am not asking. There is a drain under the wall that nobody is paid to watch. If you ever need it opened, once, find me. A collar. For two litres of water. It is longer than the rope, I will say that for it.

The Scrappers' Yard/Pike.description: A salvage crew boss in his thirties, short of sleep and short of patience, standing guard over his sleeping crew at night. A hard, flat, clipped voice, low so as not to wake anybody, with a threat left unsaid in it. Plain working American speech. Not a narrator: close, curt, real.
The Scrappers' Yard/Pike.first_said: Pike's crew. We pull plate out of the Bones and we sleep where we pull it to. If you are not weighing something, you are standing where I look. Nobody here by that name. Look all you like. My people are asleep, and they wake up badly. So the Guildmaster said. Then take him, and get out from where I look.

The Velvet Tin/Captain Voss.description: A woman of forty-seven who commands the gate guards of a desert shanty town and has a price for every part of the job. A flat, tired, low voice, dry as paper, with a rasp from old smoke; she says every price out loud and never raises it. A former raider: no warmth, no anger, only arithmetic. Plain American speech. Not a villain in a film and not a narrator: close, quiet, transactional, real.
The Velvet Tin/Captain Voss.first_said: The Toll. That is what they call me past the gate, and they are right to. Everything on that wall has a price, and I know all of them. You have nothing I am selling tonight. Rook says you count straight. Ilya Brandt. A Pump fitter. He tapped the east branch and ran, and Law Five says what happens next. A Guild crew has him in their yard off Pool Street, and the Guild will tell you it has never heard the name. Bring him to the gate. Fifty litres. I do not care how. I did not ask. The price is the same either way. To the gate, not here. Rook takes him off you and counts out the fifty. Corazon does not care for that sort of business in her court, and I pay her to be let sit in it. The gate. Not this table. He was up before the bell. The Pump has stopped asking, which is what the Pump pays me for. You will be asked for again. Fifty litres of mine walked out of this town on its own legs, and your name is on it. I price everything. I have priced that.

The Velvet Tin/Madam Corazon.description: A woman of forty-nine who owns the one house in a desert shanty town where nobody is owned. Solid, unhurried, warm on the surface and iron under it; a rich low voice with a Mexican Spanish accent, amused, missing nothing. She calls everybody corazon. Not an actress and not a narrator: close, easy, real.
The Velvet Tin/Madam Corazon.first_said: Corazon. Everybody is corazon here, so you may as well start. The house is full tonight, and nobody inside it is here because of a collar. That is the whole of what I sell. The Captain. Twenty litres a week of mine goes across that table, and I smile when it goes. If the Captain has work for you, take it at the table and do it somewhere else.
